{{Short description|none}}
A number of people have done mathematical research while imprisoned. Some were put in [[prisoner-of-war camp]]s during various conflicts, including [[World War I]] and [[World War II]]; others were forced into [[Labor camp|labour]] or [[concentration camp]]s. Several mathematicians were jailed as a result of their political views (at least in part), notably [[Évariste Galois]], [[Bertrand Russell]], and [[Chandler Davis]].

|1831–1832<ref name=":4" />
|Preface to ''Deux mémoires d’analyse pur''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Évariste Galois' Preface written in Sainte Pélagie |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Galois_Sainte_Pelagie_preface/ |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Galois |first1=Évariste |url=https://uberty.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/Peter_M._Neumann_The_Mathematical_Writings.pdf |title=The mathematical writings of Évariste Galois |last2=Neumann |first2=Peter M. |date=2011 |publisher=European mathematical society |isbn=978-3-03719-104-0 |location=Zürich |pages=2, 233}}</ref>
|Arrested during [[Bastille Day]] demonstrations; charged with wearing a police uniform and carrying a firearm.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4">{{cite journal |last1=Rothman |first1=Tony |title=Genius and Biographers: The Fictionalization of Evariste Galois |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |date=1982 |volume=89 |issue=2 |pages=84–106 |doi=10.2307/2320923 |jstor=2320923 |quote=The cause for Galois's second arrest was preventive: On Bastille Day, July 14, 1831, he and his republican friend Duchatelet were apprehended dressed in Artillery Guard uniforms and heavily armed. Because the Artillery Guard had been disbanded on the last day of 1830 in fear of its becoming an instrument of the republicans, to wear the uniform was an outright gesture of defiance. It was also illegal. This was the charge brought against Galois, but not until the late date of October 23; he was sentenced to six months in prison. The sentence was confirmed by the court of appeals on December 3. In the meantime, Galois had been sitting in Sainte-Pélagie prison since his arrest in July.}}</ref>{{Efn|Previously arrested for alleged threats against [[Louis Philippe I|King Louis Philippe I]].<ref name=":0" />}}

|[[André Weil]]
|{{Ill|Rouen Prison|fr|Maison d'arrêt de Rouen}}<ref name=":7" />
|1940<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Knapp |first=Anthony W |date=April 1999 |title=André Weil: A Prologue |url=https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~aknapp/pdf-files/weil.pdf |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |volume=46 |issue=4 |pages=438 |quote=He and Eveline accepted an invitation from Lars Ahlfors to visit the Ahlfors family in Finland. A little later he was jailed in Finland as a spy, was spared execution because of efforts by Nevanlinna, and was deported to Sweden. He spent time in jails successively in Sweden, England, and finally France, ending up in Rouen in February 1940. The time in jail in Rouen was a particularly productive one for him mathematically; it was when he proved the Riemann hypothesis for curves over finite fields, edited the proof sheets for his integration book, and made progress on his draft of a Bourbaki volume on integration.}}</ref>
|Proof of the [[Riemann hypothesis for curves over finite fields]]<ref name=":2" />
